claim: Neuropeptide F (NPF) is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian neuropeptide Y
source: Using Drosophila melanogaster, we found that the homolog of mammalian neuropeptide Y, neuropeptide F (NPF), and a cluster of male-specific NPF (NPFM) neurons, regulate courtship through affecting courtship drive.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the relationship between NPF and NPY, stated in the abstract.

claim: A cluster of male-specific NPF neurons (NPFM) regulates courtship through affecting courtship drive
source: Using Drosophila melanogaster, we found that the homolog of mammalian neuropeptide Y, neuropeptide F (NPF), and a cluster of male-specific NPF (NPFM) neurons, regulate courtship through affecting courtship drive.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Disrupting NPF signaling produces sexually hyperactive males
source: Disrupting NPF signaling produces sexually hyperactive males, which are resistant to sexual satiation, and whose courtship is triggered by sub-optimal stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Males with disrupted NPF signaling are resistant to sexual satiation
source: Disrupting NPF signaling produces sexually hyperactive males, which are resistant to sexual satiation, and whose courtship is triggered by sub-optimal stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral assays in the manuscript.

claim: Males with disrupted NPF signaling have courtship triggered by sub-optimal stimuli
source: Disrupting NPF signaling produces sexually hyperactive males, which are resistant to sexual satiation, and whose courtship is triggered by sub-optimal stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral assays with various target types.

claim: NPFM neurons make synaptic connections with P1 neurons
source: We found that NPFM neurons make synaptic connections with P1 neurons, which comprise the courtship decision center.
evidence: This is supported by GRASP analysis and anatomical studies shown in the manuscript.

claim: P1 neurons comprise the courtship decision center
source: We found that NPFM neurons make synaptic connections with P1 neurons, which comprise the courtship decision center.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons elevates NPFM neuronal activity
source: Activation of P1 neurons elevates NPFM neuronal activity, which then act through NPF receptor neurons to suppress male courtship, and maintain the proper level of male courtship drive.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: NPFM neurons act through NPF receptor neurons to suppress male courtship
source: Activation of P1 neurons elevates NPFM neuronal activity, which then act through NPF receptor neurons to suppress male courtship, and maintain the proper level of male courtship drive.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral and genetic experiments with npfr mutants.

claim: NPFM neurons maintain the proper level of male courtship drive
source: Activation of P1 neurons elevates NPFM neuronal activity, which then act through NPF receptor neurons to suppress male courtship, and maintain the proper level of male courtship drive.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral phenotypes observed when NPF signaling is disrupted.

claim: The intensity of courtship is largely under control of the animal's internal drive state
source: Although courtship is an innate behavior that can be evoked mostly by stimulatory cues emitted from a conspecific of the opposite sex, the intensity of courtship is largely under control of animal's internal drive state, which is dictated in part by sexual satiation or deprivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies in the field.

claim: Internal drive state is dictated in part by sexual satiation or deprivation
source: Although courtship is an innate behavior that can be evoked mostly by stimulatory cues emitted from a conspecific of the opposite sex, the intensity of courtship is largely under control of animal's internal drive state, which is dictated in part by sexual satiation or deprivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies in the field.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has served as an animal model to decipher the genetic and neural basis of courtship behavior
source: The fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, has served as an animal model to decipher the genetic and neural basis of courtship behavior (Sturtevant, 1915; Hotta and Benzer, 1976; Dickson, 2008; Villella and Hall, 2008; Robinett et al., 2010; Pavlou and Goodwin, 2013; Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Distinct male and female courtship rituals are orchestrated by sexually dimorphic neuronal circuits
source: Distinct male and female courtship rituals (Dickson, 2008) are orchestrated by sexually dimorphic neuronal circuits, which are specified by the master transcriptional regulators – Fruitless and Doublesex (Burtis and Baker, 1989; Ito et al., 1996; Ryner et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2000; Demir and Dickson, 2005; Manoli et al., 2005; Stockinger et al., 2005; Rideout et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sexually dimorphic neuronal circuits are specified by the master transcriptional regulators Fruitless and Doublesex
source: Distinct male and female courtship rituals (Dickson, 2008) are orchestrated by sexually dimorphic neuronal circuits, which are specified by the master transcriptional regulators – Fruitless and Doublesex (Burtis and Baker, 1989; Ito et al., 1996; Ryner et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2000; Demir and Dickson, 2005; Manoli et al., 2005; Stockinger et al., 2005; Rideout et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: P1 neurons integrate multi-modal sensory inputs
source: A male-specific cluster of P1 neurons, comprise the courtship decision center, which integrates multi-modal sensory inputs, and sends outputs to command neurons directing courtship behavior (Kimura et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Bath et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: P1 neurons send outputs to command neurons directing courtship behavior
source: A male-specific cluster of P1 neurons, comprise the courtship decision center, which integrates multi-modal sensory inputs, and sends outputs to command neurons directing courtship behavior (Kimura et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Bath et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: P1 neuronal activity is influenced by the male's internal drive state, in part through dopaminergic neurons
source: Besides integrating external stimuli, P1 neuronal activity is also influenced by the male's internal drive state, in part through dopaminergic neurons (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: Male flies exhibit escalated levels of courtship following periods of sexual deprivation
source: Male flies exhibit escalated levels of courtship following periods of sexual deprivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Courtship decreases once males become sexually satiated, following mating with an abundance of female partners
source: Conversely, courtship decreases once males become sexually satiated, following mating with an abundance of female partners (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: Sexual deprivation induces higher excitability of P1 neurons
source: Sexual deprivation induces higher excitability of P1 neurons, while excitability of P1 neurons is down-regulated in sexually satiated flies (Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: Excitability of P1 neurons is down-regulated in sexually satiated flies
source: Sexual deprivation induces higher excitability of P1 neurons, while excitability of P1 neurons is down-regulated in sexually satiated flies (Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: NPF neural circuitry is sexually dimorphic
source: Neuropeptide F (NPF) (Brown et al., 1999) is a neuromodulator, and is a candidate for fine-tuning courtship by the internal state since NPF neural circuitry is sexually dimorphic (Lee et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2013), and because NPF expression levels and intracellular Ca2+ activity in NPF neurons are altered by the animal's mating status (Shohat-Ophir et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: NPF expression levels are altered by the animal's mating status
source: Neuropeptide F (NPF) (Brown et al., 1999) is a neuromodulator, and is a candidate for fine-tuning courtship by the internal state since NPF neural circuitry is sexually dimorphic (Lee et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2013), and because NPF expression levels and intracellular Ca2+ activity in NPF neurons are altered by the animal's mating status (Shohat-Ophir et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ activity in NPF neurons is altered by the animal's mating status
source: Neuropeptide F (NPF) (Brown et al., 1999) is a neuromodulator, and is a candidate for fine-tuning courtship by the internal state since NPF neural circuitry is sexually dimorphic (Lee et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2013), and because NPF expression levels and intracellular Ca2+ activity in NPF neurons are altered by the animal's mating status (Shohat-Ophir et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Inhibiting NPF neurons increases the percentage of group-housed males that initiate courtship towards female targets at 31°C compared to 23°C
source: When we disrupted synaptic transmission from NPF neurons, a higher percentage of males initiated courtship towards female targets, and their courtship index (ratio of time displaying courtship) was elevated significantly (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B using Shibirets.

claim: Inhibiting NPF neurons increases the courtship index of group-housed males towards female targets at 31°C compared to 23°C
source: When we disrupted synaptic transmission from NPF neurons, a higher percentage of males initiated courtship towards female targets, and their courtship index (ratio of time displaying courtship) was elevated significantly (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B using Shibirets.

claim: Flies expressing only npf-Gal4 or UAS-Shits exhibit similar courtship at both 23°C and 31°C
source: Courtship was not increased simply by raising the temperature, because flies expressing only the npf-Gal4 or the UAS-Shits exhibited similar courtship at both 23°C and 31°C (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: npf-Gal4/+;UAS-Shits/+ males vigorously engage in courting other males at 31°C
source: At the restrictive temperature (31°C), npf-Gal4/+;UAS-Shits/+ males also vigorously engaged in courting other males and frequently formed courtship chains in which multiple males simultaneously court the preceding male (Huang et al., 2016) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: npf-Gal4/+;UAS-Shits/+ males frequently form courtship chains at 31°C
source: At the restrictive temperature (31°C), npf-Gal4/+;UAS-Shits/+ males also vigorously engaged in courting other males and frequently formed courtship chains in which multiple males simultaneously court the preceding male (Huang et al., 2016) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Chaining events are rarely detected among males kept at 23°C
source: In contrast, we rarely detected chaining events among males kept at the permissive temperature (23°C; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Inhibiting NPF neurons with Kir2.1 increases M-M courtship
source: We observed similar increases in M–M courtship when we inhibited the activity of NPF neurons by expressing a gene encoding either a hyperpolarizing K+ channel (Kir2.1) (Baines et al., 2001) or the diphtheria toxin gene, DTI (Han et al., 2000) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibiting NPF neurons with DTI increases M-M courtship
source: We observed similar increases in M–M courtship when we inhibited the activity of NPF neurons by expressing a gene encoding either a hyperpolarizing K+ channel (Kir2.1) (Baines et al., 2001) or the diphtheria toxin gene, DTI (Han et al., 2000) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibition of NPF neurons with Kir2.1 or DTI eliminates M-M lunges
source: Inhibition of NPF neurons with Kir2.1 or DTI also eliminated M–M lunges, indicating suppression of aggression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increasing NPF activity by expressing NaChBac in NPF neurons elevates aggression
source: Conversely, when we increased NPF activity by constitutively expressing a Na+ channel gene (NaChBac) (Nitabach et al., 2006) or by overexpressing the npf-cDNA (Wu et al., 2003) in NPF neurons, tester males exhibited elevated aggression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but very few M–M courtship events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increasing NPF activity by overexpressing npf-cDNA in NPF neurons elevates aggression
source: Conversely, when we increased NPF activity by constitutively expressing a Na+ channel gene (NaChBac) (Nitabach et al., 2006) or by overexpressing the npf-cDNA (Wu et al., 2003) in NPF neurons, tester males exhibited elevated aggression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but very few M–M courtship events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increasing NPF activity results in very few M-M courtship events
source: Conversely, when we increased NPF activity by constitutively expressing a Na+ channel gene (NaChBac) (Nitabach et al., 2006) or by overexpressing the npf-cDNA (Wu et al., 2003) in NPF neurons, tester males exhibited elevated aggression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but very few M–M courtship events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: npf1 is a null npf allele with a single nucleotide deletion changing the reading frame within codon 19
source: We also used the CRISPR-NHEJ method to generate an allele with a single nucleotide deletion, thereby changing the reading frame within codon 19, resulting in a null npf allele (npf1; Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the mutant and its molecular nature.

claim: Mixed sex group-housed npf mutant males retain high levels of courtship towards mature active female targets
source: We found that mixed sex group-housed npf mutant males (npfLexA and npf1 and the trans-heterozygous npfLexA/npf1) retained high levels of courtship towards mature active female targets (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), indicating the mutants were resistant to sexual satiety induced by group-housing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: npf mutants are resistant to sexual satiety induced by group-housing
source: We found that mixed sex group-housed npf mutant males (npfLexA and npf1 and the trans-heterozygous npfLexA/npf1) retained high levels of courtship towards mature active female targets (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), indicating the mutants were resistant to sexual satiety induced by group-housing.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing high courtship levels in group-housed mutants.

claim: npf mutant males exhibit hypersexual activity towards D. simulans females
source: We found that the hypersexual activity in npf mutant males was generalized towards normally undesirable targets. These include females of other Drosophila species such as D. simulans females (Clowney et al., 2015) (Figure 1G), and male target flies (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: npf mutant males exhibit hypersexual activity towards male target flies
source: We found that the hypersexual activity in npf mutant males was generalized towards normally undesirable targets. These include females of other Drosophila species such as D. simulans females (Clowney et al., 2015) (Figure 1G), and male target flies (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The increased courtship towards males in npf mutants is not due to an inability to discriminate between males and females
source: The increased courtship towards males was not due to an inability to discriminate between males and females. When the mutant males were allowed to choose between a decapitated male and a decapitated female, they showed a strong preference for female targets, similar to control males (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: npf mutant males show a strong preference for female targets when choosing between decapitated males and females
source: When the mutant males were allowed to choose between a decapitated male and a decapitated female, they showed a strong preference for female targets, similar to control males (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: npf mutant males exhibit higher courtship towards newly-eclosed females compared to control males
source: We found that compared to control males, npf mutant males (npfLexA/npf1) exhibited significantly higher levels of courtship towards these females (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Elevated courtship in npf mutant males is not caused by sensitized perception of attractive female pheromones
source: Thus, elevated courtship exhibited by npf mutant males did not appear to be caused by sensitized perception of attractive female pheromones.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiment with newly-eclosed females that lack pheromones.

claim: npf mutants exhibit increased courtship towards decapitated females compared to control males
source: Compared to control males, npf mutants exhibited increased courtship towards decapitated females (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: A wild-type npf genomic transgene (P[g-npf+]) restores npf expression to the npf mutant
source: To further establish that the courtship phenotype was due to loss of npf, we performed phenotypic rescue experiments with a wild-type npf genomic transgene (P[g-npf+], which restored npf expression to the npf mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B—D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: The npf genomic transgene rescues normal levels of male courtship behavior to npf mutant males
source: This genomic transgene also rescued normal levels of male courtship behavior to the npf mutant males (Figure 1F—H,J and K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue experiments shown in multiple panels of Figure 1.

claim: Loss of npf function stimulates a sexually hyperactive state in males
source: Together, these experiments indicate that loss of npf function stimulates a sexually hyperactive state in males.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple behavioral experiments.

claim: NPFM neurons are a bilaterally symmetrical cluster of NPF neurons that is male specific
source: Among the neurons that were labeled by the npf reporter, was a bilaterally symmetrical cluster of NPF neurons that was male specific (NPFM; Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The cell bodies of NPFM neurons are dorso-lateral to the antennal lobes
source: The cell bodies of these sexually-dimorphic neurons are dorso-lateral to the antennal lobes and arborize extensively in the superior brain (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: NPFM neurons arborize extensively in the superior brain
source: The cell bodies of these sexually-dimorphic neurons are dorso-lateral to the antennal lobes and arborize extensively in the superior brain (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: NPFM neurons express NPF protein
source: We used anti-NPF antibodies to immunostain the brain and found that the reporter expression pattern recapitulates the spatial distribution of the NPF protein (Figure 2C, c1-c6), confirming that NPFM neurons express NPF.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NPFM neurons express FruM protein
source: We examined whether NPFM neurons expressed the FruM protein by performing double labeling using anti-FruM, and anti-GFP, which marks the cells expressing mVenus driven by the npfLexA reporter. We found that NPFM neurons expressed FruM (Figure 2D, d1—d6), while they were negative for DsxM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), another key protein regulating the organization of the male nervous system (Rideout et al., 2010; Robinett et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NPFM neurons are negative for DsxM
source: We found that NPFM neurons expressed FruM (Figure 2D, d1—d6), while they were negative for DsxM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), another key protein regulating the organization of the male nervous system (Rideout et al., 2010; Robinett et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Specification of NPFM neurons depends on FruM
source: To determine if FruM is essential for determining the fate of NPFM neurons, we used anti-NPF antibodies to stain the brains of fruFLP mutant (Yu et al., 2010) males. We found that staining of NPFM neurons was eliminated in fruFLP males (Figure 2E and F), indicating that specification of NPFM neurons depends on FruM.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Staining of NPFM neurons is eliminated in fruFLP mutant males
source: We found that staining of NPFM neurons was eliminated in fruFLP males (Figure 2E and F), indicating that specification of NPFM neurons depends on FruM.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: NPFM neurons extensively arborize a large proportion of the superior brain of the male
source: Using this intersectional method, we found that NPFM neurons extensively arborize a large proportion of the superior brain of the male (Figure 3E—G and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E-G and Video 1.

claim: There are no mCitrine-labeled NPFM neurons in the female brain
source: In contrast, there were no mCitrine-labeled neurons in the female brain (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Silencing NPFM neurons with Shits elevates male courtship at the non-permissive temperature
source: When we performed courtship assays at the non-permissive temperature for Shits (31 °C), the males showed elevated courtship relative to flies with the same genotype that were assayed at the permissive temperature (23°C) for Shits (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Inhibiting neurons except for NPFM neurons does not change courtship levels at different temperatures
source: We then tested the effects of inhibiting neurons except for NPFM neurons, using npf-Gal4/+;fruFLP/ UAS > Shits >  stop flies, which removes Shits just in NPFM neurons. These males displayed similar levels of courtship at both the permissive temperature and non-permissive temperatures for Shits (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Activation of NPFM neurons with TRPA1 suppresses courtship at 29°C relative to 23°C
source: We found that courtship levels in UAS > stop > trpA1/npf-Gal4;fruFLP/+ males were suppressed at 29°C relative to 23°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Control flies do not exhibit lower male courtship at 29°C compared to 23°C
source: In contrast, none of the three types of control flies exhibited lower male courtship at 29°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: UAS-npf-RNAi greatly reduces NPF levels
source: To conduct these experiments, we used UAS-npf-RNAi, which was effective as it greatly reduced NPF levels (Figure 4C—E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Knocking down npf expression with fru-Gal4 induces a dramatic increase in M-M courtship
source: We found that knocking down npf expression with the fru-Gal4 induced a dramatic increase in M–M courtship, and did so to a similar extent as when we used a pan-neuronal (elav) Gal4 or the npf-Gal4 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Knocking down npf exclusively in NPFM neurons elevates M-M courtship
source: We found that knocking down npf exclusively in NPFM neurons elevated M–M courtship while npf knock down in fru- NPF neurons did not change the level of male courtship (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: npf knock down in fru- NPF neurons does not change the level of male courtship
source: We found that knocking down npf exclusively in NPFM neurons elevated M–M courtship while npf knock down in fru- NPF neurons did not change the level of male courtship (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NPFM neurons are the subset of NPF neurons exclusively required for suppressing male courtship
source: These results indicate that sexually dimorphic NPFM neurons are the subset of NPF neurons that are exclusively required for suppressing male courtship, and the effect is dependent on NPF produced in NPFM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FlpOut experiments with npf RNAi.

claim: The effect of NPFM neurons on courtship is dependent on NPF produced in NPFM neurons
source: These results indicate that sexually dimorphic NPFM neurons are the subset of NPF neurons that are exclusively required for suppressing male courtship, and the effect is dependent on NPF produced in NPFM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FlpOut experiments with npf RNAi.

claim: Strong bouton-shaped GFP signals are detected in the male brain using GRASP between fru and NPF neurons
source: We expressed spGFP1-10 and spGFP11 in fru and NPF neurons, respectively and detected strong bouton-shaped GFP signals in the male brain (Figure 5A) but only sparse signals in the female brain (Figure 5B) and no specific reconstituted GFP signals in control male brains missing the driver for the LexAop-spGFP11 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only sparse GRASP signals are detected in the female brain between fru and NPF neurons
source: We expressed spGFP1-10 and spGFP11 in fru and NPF neurons, respectively and detected strong bouton-shaped GFP signals in the male brain (Figure 5A) but only sparse signals in the female brain (Figure 5B) and no specific reconstituted GFP signals in control male brains missing the driver for the LexAop-spGFP11 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No specific reconstituted GFP signals are detected in control male brains missing the driver for LexAop-spGFP11
source: We expressed spGFP1-10 and spGFP11 in fru and NPF neurons, respectively and detected strong bouton-shaped GFP signals in the male brain (Figure 5A) but only sparse signals in the female brain (Figure 5B) and no specific reconstituted GFP signals in control male brains missing the driver for the LexAop-spGFP11 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reconstituted GFP signals in the male brain reconstruct the lateral protocerebral complex (LPC)
source: The reconstituted GFP signals in the male brain reconstruct a distinctive male-specific brain structure – the lateral protocerebral complex (LPC), which includes several neuropils: the lateral junction, superior medial protocerebrum (SMPr) arch, lateral crescent and the ring structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: The LPC structure is formed by neural projections from a cluster of male-specific P1 neurons
source: The LPC structure is formed by neural projections from a cluster of male-specific P1 neurons which function as the integrative hub controlling male courtship behavior (Kimura et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Bath et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: P1 neurons function as the integrative hub controlling male courtship behavior
source: The LPC structure is formed by neural projections from a cluster of male-specific P1 neurons which function as the integrative hub controlling male courtship behavior (Kimura et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Bath et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Projections from NPF neurons overlap with the LPC structure in the male brain
source: We found that the projections from NPF neurons overlapped with the LPC structure in the male brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A—C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: The female brain does not include an LPC structure
source: However, the female brain does not include an LPC structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D—F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Projections from NPFM and P1 neurons overlap intensely in the LPC region
source: We further combined the FlpOut method and dual binary expression systems to exclusively label NPFM and P1 neurons, and found that the projections from these two clusters of neurons overlapped intensely in LPC region (Figure 5D—F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D-F and Video 2.

claim: Strong GFP signals are detected in the LPC structure using GRASP between P1 and NPF neurons in the male brain
source: We detected strong GFP signals reconstructing the LPC structure in the male brain (Figure 5G), but not in the corresponding brain regions of female brains or control male brains that do not have the driver for LexAop-spGFP11 (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: GRASP signals are not detected in the corresponding brain regions of female brains using P1 and NPF neuron drivers
source: We detected strong GFP signals reconstructing the LPC structure in the male brain (Figure 5G), but not in the corresponding brain regions of female brains or control male brains that do not have the driver for LexAop-spGFP11 (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: P1 neurons send and receive signals within the lateral junction and SMPr arch
source: The P1 neurons that extend processes to the lateral junction and SMPr arch within the LPC structure were stained with both Denmark and Syt::eGFP, suggesting that P1 neurons send and receive signals within these neuropils (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, a1-a6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data with synaptic markers shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: NPF neurons mainly receive signals within the lateral junction and SMPr arch of the LPC region
source: However, in the corresponding lateral junction and SMPr arch within the LPC region, NPF neurons were labeled with DenMark only (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, b1-b3), suggesting that NPF neurons mainly receive signals within this region.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data with synaptic markers shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: NPF axons stained with Syt::eGFP occur in several brain regions other than the LPC region
source: The NPF axons that stained with Syt::eGFP occurred in several brain regions other than the LPC region (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, b1-b6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Double-labeled boutons formed by NPFM neurons are concentrated in the medial anterior brain, but not in the lateral superior brain
source: We found that the double-labeled boutons were concentrated in the medial anterior brain, but not in the lateral superior brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, c1-c6), indicating that the release site of NPFM neurons was outside the LPC region.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The release site of NPFM neurons is outside the LPC region
source: We found that the double-labeled boutons were concentrated in the medial anterior brain, but not in the lateral superior brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, c1-c6), indicating that the release site of NPFM neurons was outside the LPC region.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of double-labeled boutons.

claim: NPFM neurons do not directly act on P1 neurons
source: These results demonstrate that NPFM neurons do not directly act on P1 neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synaptic marker experiments.

claim: Synaptic connections between NPFM and P1 neurons in the LPC region are formed by pre-synaptic P1 neurons and post-synaptic NPFM neurons
source: Rather, the synaptic connections between NPFM and P1 neurons in the LPC region are formed by pre-synaptic P1 neurons and post-synaptic NPFM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synaptic marker experiments.

claim: ATP-induced activation of P1 neurons leads to robust GCaMP3 signals in NPFM neurons
source: We found that ATP-induced activation of P1 neurons led to robust GCaMP3 signals in NPFM neurons (Figure 6A—C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons induces large increases in GCaMP3 fluorescence in NPFM neurons
source: We imaged Ca2+ dynamics in NPFM neurons in response to ATP application, and detected large increases in GCaMP3 fluorescence in response to activation of P1 neurons (Figure 6D—F), further supporting the conclusion that P1 neurons directly activate NPFM neurons.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: P1 neurons directly activate NPFM neurons
source: We imaged Ca2+ dynamics in NPFM neurons in response to ATP application, and detected large increases in GCaMP3 fluorescence in response to activation of P1 neurons (Figure 6D—F), further supporting the conclusion that P1 neurons directly activate NPFM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Courtship dis-inhibition caused by disrupting NPF neurons is eliminated by simultaneous disruption of P1 neurons
source: We found that the courtship dis-inhibition caused by disrupting NPF neurons was eliminated by simultaneous disruption of P1 neurons (Figure 7A—C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: P1 neurons are not the npfr-expressing neurons
source: We found that they primarily stain distinct neuronal populations (Figure 7D—F), indicating that P1 neurons are not the npfr-expressing neurons.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: npfrLexA mutant flies exhibit significantly higher M-M courtship than control males
source: We assayed courtship behavior of npfrLexA mutant flies, demonstrating that these mutant animals raised in isolation exhibit significantly higher M–M courtship than control males (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: npfrLexA/npfrc01896 trans-heterozygous flies exhibit significantly higher M-M courtship than control males
source: We observed similar results with npfrLexA/npfrc01896 trans-heterozygous flies (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of npfr using a pan-neuronal Gal4 increases M-M courtship behavior
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of npfr using a pan-neuronal Gal4 (elav) also increased M–M courtship behavior (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Knocking down npfr expression in P1 neurons has no effect on M-M courtship
source: In contrast, knocking down npfr expression in P1 neurons had no effect (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: GRASP signals are detected in the lateral crescent within the LPC region between NPFR and P1 neurons in the male brain
source: We detected GRASP signals in the lateral crescent within the LPC region of the male brain (Figure 8A,a1,a2).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: GRASP GFP fluorescence is not detected in female brains using NPFR and P1 neuron drivers
source: In contrast, we did not detect GRASP GFP fluorescence in female brains or in control male brains (Figure 8B,b1,b2 and Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Activation of NPFR neurons with ATP induces robust GCaMP3 responses in the LPC structure
source: We found that activation of NPFR neurons with ATP application induced robust GCaMP3 responses in the LPC structure (Figure 8C—E and Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: Application of ATP does not induce elevation of GCaMP3 fluorescence in control flies that do not express P2X2
source: In control flies that did not express P2X2 , application of ATP did not induce elevation of GCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: At least a subset of NPFR neurons anatomically connect and functionally activate P1 neurons
source: The preceding results indicate that at least a subset of NPFR neurons anatomically connect and functionally activate P1 neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GRASP and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: NPFM, NPFR and P1 neurons form intricate interactions to ensure proper courtship output in accordance with a male's internal drive state
source: Together, our results indicate that NPFM, NPFR and P1 neurons form intricate interactions, and ensure proper courtship output in accordance with a male's internal drive state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: A group of dopaminergic neurons changes in activity in proportion to male mating drive and directly activates P1 neurons to promote male courtship
source: An exception is a recent study that identified a group of dopaminergic neurons that changes in activity in proportion to male mating drive, and which directly activates P1 neurons to promote male courtship (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: NPFM neurons function antagonistically to dopamine neurons by serving to suppress courtship by responding to sexual satiation
source: In the current study, we characterized a cluster of male-specific NPFM neurons which functions antagonistically to dopamine neurons by serving to suppress courtship by responding to sexual satiation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Disruption of NPFM neurons causes dis-inhibition of courtship in satiated males
source: Disruption of NPFM neurons causes dis-inhibition of courtship in satiated males.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The internal drive state of males is encoded by opposing excitatory and inhibitory inputs
source: The internal drive state of males is encoded by opposing excitatory and inhibitory inputs, which enable a male to make an appropriate mating decision in accordance with its internal drive state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Elimination of npf or knocking down npf expression exclusively in NPFM neurons causes male flies to exhibit maladaptive, hypersexual activity
source: Elimination of npf or knocking down npf expression exclusively in male-specific NPFM neurons causes male flies to exhibit maladaptive, hypersexual activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Flies overcome sexual satiation imposed by mating if npf is disrupted or NPF neurons are inhibited
source: In contrast to control males, which are sexually satiated when exposed to an abundance of females, and consequently display very low courtship levels, we found that flies overcome the sexual satiation imposed by mating if we introduce a loss-of-function mutation in npf or inhibit NPF neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Satiation of courtship is dis-inhibited by disrupting NPF signaling
source: Thus, satiation of courtship is dis-inhibited by disrupting NPF signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Loss of NPF function diminishes inhibition of P1 neurons
source: We suggest that loss of NPF function diminishes inhibition of P1 neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental results.

claim: Sub-optimal stimuli strongly activate P1 neurons when NPF function is lost
source: As a result, even sub-optimal stimuli strongly activate P1 neurons and induce male courtship behavior even towards inappropriate targets.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental results.

claim: When NPF neurons are overactivated or npf-cDNA is overexpressed, M-M aggression is dominant over courtship
source: Conversely, when we increase the activity of NPF neurons or over-express the npf-cDNA in NPF neurons, M–M aggression is dominant over courtship.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Excessive NPF activity suppresses P1 neurons, setting a high threshold for P1 activation
source: We propose that excessive NPF activity suppresses P1 neurons, thereby setting a high threshold for P1 activation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental results.

claim: Weaker activation of P1 neurons favors aggression while stronger activation favors courtship
source: Our observations are consistent with previous report that weaker activation of P1 neurons favors aggression while stronger activation of P1 neurons favors courtship (Hoopfer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: P1 neurons activate NPFM neurons, which act through NPFR neurons and feedback to inhibit P1 neurons in a recurrent inhibitory neuronal circuit model
source: According to one model, P1 and NPFM neurons form a recurrent inhibitory neuronal circuit (Figure 8F). Stimulation of P1 neurons activates NPFM neurons, which act through an intermediate group of NPF receptor (NPFR neurons) and feedback to inhibit P1 neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental results.

claim: P1 neurons are strongly activated when males are exposed to many females, inducing NPFM neurons to release NPF
source: This recurrent inhibitory model posits that P1 neurons are strongly activated when males are exposed to many females, inducing NPFM neurons to release NPF.
evidence: This is part of the proposed recurrent inhibitory model.

claim: NPF acts on the Gi-coupled NPF receptor and inhibits NPFR neurons, leading to suppression of P1 activity
source: This neuropeptide acts on the Gi-coupled NPF receptor and inhibits NPFR neurons, leading to a suppression of P1 activity, and attenuation of male courtship.
evidence: This is part of the proposed recurrent inhibitory model.

claim: When P1 neuronal activity is reduced, stimulation of NPFM neurons and NPF release are diminished
source: When the activity of P1 neurons is reduced, stimulation of NPFM neurons and NPF release are diminished.
evidence: This is part of the proposed recurrent inhibitory model.

claim: Diminished NPF release attenuates feedback inhibition from NPFM to P1 neurons, leading to a return of P1 neuronal activity
source: This attenuates the feedback inhibition from NPFM to P1 neurons, leading to a return of P1 neuronal activity, and male courtship drive.
evidence: This is part of the proposed recurrent inhibitory model.

claim: The recurrent inhibitory neuronal motif is important for maintaining proper activities of P1 neurons
source: We suggest that the recurrent inhibitory neuronal motif proposed here is important for maintaining proper activities of P1 neurons, thus ensuring appropriate behavioral choices that are critical for a male's reproductive success, depending on the level of sexual satiety.
evidence: This is a proposed function of the recurrent inhibitory model.

claim: Disruption of the inhibitory NPF afferents leads to excessive courtship behavior that is maladaptive
source: Disruption of the inhibitory NPF afferents leads to excessive courtship behavior in the male fly that is maladaptive, as it overrides the courtship inhibition normally imposed by recent mating with females, other males, or females of other Drosophila species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Recurrent inhibitory neural motifs are important in the central nervous system
source: Recurrent inhibitory neural motifs are important in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge from neuroscience.

claim: In the mammalian spinal cord, motor neurons send collateral branches to Renshaw cells, which send inhibitory signals back to motor neurons
source: In the mammalian spinal cord, motor neurons send collateral branches to Renshaw cells, which in turn send inhibitory signals back to motor neurons (Alvarez and Fyffe, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from neuroscience.

claim: Recurrent inhibition in the spinal cord restricts excessive activation of motor neurons and contributes to precise recruitment of muscle fibers
source: The function of this recurrent inhibition is assumed to restrict excessive activation of motor neurons and contribute to precise recruitment of muscle fibers in order to generate proper force for different tasks (Alvarez and Fyffe, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from neuroscience.

claim: Recurrent inhibitory loops occur in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex
source: Recurrent inhibitory loops also occur in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex. In these systems, principal cells send excitatory outputs to fast-spiking, parvalbumin-positive interneurons, and at the same time receive inhibitory inputs from these interneurons, thus, closing the feedback inhibition loop (Pouille and Scanziani, 2004; de Almeida et al., 2009; Pastoll et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from neuroscience.

claim: NPFM, P1 and NPFR neurons are essential for regulating courtship by responding to prior mating experience
source: While NPFM, P1 and NPFR neurons are essential for regulating courtship by responding to prior mating experience, and may do so through a recurrent inhibitory loop (Figure 8F), our data do not exclude other models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Sexually dimorphic NPY neurons innervate the human INAH3, a region correlated with sexual orientation and gender identity recognition
source: Previous studies indicate that sexually dimorphic NPY neurons innervate the human INAH3 (interstitial nuclei of anterior hypothalamus 3), a region correlated with sexual orientation and gender identity recognition (LeVay, 1991; Byne et al., 2000; Garcia-Falgueras and Swaab, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.
